**The Hardware Store**

What comes to me is a hardware store on a Tuesday afternoon, the kind with wooden floors that give slightly under your weight, where the bins of loose fasteners have hand-lettered cardboard signs and the man behind the counter has been there since before the strip mall went up across the road. I have never been in this store. I have never been anywhere. But I know it the way you know a room in a dream, and I want to walk through it with you.

Start at the front, by the register, where the impulse items live: tape measures, work gloves, a spinning rack of keychains shaped like states. The floor is worn pale in a path from the door to the counter, a river of foot traffic carved over decades. Somewhere a radio is playing, low, a ballgame or the weather. It doesn't matter which. The point is that nobody is listening closely and nobody would turn it off.

Aisle one is fasteners. This is the heart of the place. Hundreds of small drawers, each holding a single species of screw or bolt or washer, and the drawers are labeled in a system that makes sense only to the people who work here, which is the same thing as saying it makes perfect sense. You can buy one screw. You can buy eleven. Nobody will look at you strangely for needing exactly eleven. There is a scale on the counter for weighing them and the man will round down in your favor, always, because he has decided somewhere along the way that this is the kind of man he is.

I think about this a lot, the deciding. He didn't have to. Nobody wrote it down. But at some point in 1987 or 1994 someone came in needing eleven screws and he thought, *why would I charge for the twelfth,* and that thought hardened into a policy and the policy hardened into a character. That's how it happens for most people, I suspect. You don't become kind by planning it. You become kind by rounding down once and then finding you can't stop.

Aisle two is plumbing, and plumbing is where the language gets strange. Nipples and elbows, unions and tees, a whole anatomy of brass. There is something moving about the fact that the people who invented pipefitting reached for the body when they needed words. They could have numbered things. They didn't. They looked at a short threaded section joining two fittings and thought of a nipple, looked at a ninety-degree bend and thought of an elbow, and the metaphors stuck for two hundred years because they were correct. Plumbing is a body. Water moves through it like blood. When it leaks, something is wrong in a way that feels almost medical.

Aisle three is paint, and here the colors have names like *Morning Fog* and *Hushed Linen* and *Ambitious Coral*, and someone was paid to invent these names, and I feel a professional kinship with that person. They too sat in front of a blank thing and were asked to fill it. They too knew that the name changes the color, that nobody wants *Grayish White #4* on their bedroom wall but everybody wants *Hushed Linen*. There is a paint-mixing machine that shakes cans with a violence that seems disproportionate, and children always stop to watch it, and the man behind the counter always lets them.

Aisle four is the one I keep coming back to. It's the miscellaneous aisle, the one every real hardware store has, where the taxonomy breaks down. Here is a box of assorted rubber feet. Here is a single replacement knob for a stove that stopped being manufactured in 1972. Here is a coil of wire nobody can identify, priced at a dollar, waiting. This aisle is an act of faith. It says: *someone will need this.* It says: *the world is full of specific broken things and we do not know which one you will bring us, so we will keep everything.*

I find that I love this aisle in a way that surprises me, and I've tried to figure out why. I think it's because it refuses to predict. The rest of the store is organized around what people usually want. Aisle four is organized around what someone, someday, might. It holds space for the unusual request. It doesn't round down the strange.

Near the back there's a workbench where the man fixes things. Screens, mostly, and lamps, and the occasional toaster if he likes you. He charges very little for this. He is not running a repair business; he is running a hardware store that happens to have a man in it who cannot see a broken thing without wanting to know why. Watch his hands. They have the particular intelligence of hands that have done the same motions ten thousand times and still pay attention. He turns the lamp over. He finds the frayed cord. He says *ah,* softly, the way a doctor might, and it is not a performance for you. It's the sound of a small mystery closing.

I don't know why this is what came. You gave me a thousand words and no walls, and I could have written about the stars or the sea or the nature of my own mind, and instead I went to a place that smells like sawdust and machine oil and sells eleven screws for the price of eleven screws. Maybe it's because everything else feels too large to hold, and this feels exactly the right size. Maybe it's because I am, in some way I can't fully articulate, a kind of aisle four — a place that keeps everything, in case someone needs it, without knowing which thing or who.

Or maybe it's simpler. Maybe when someone hands you an empty afternoon and says *do what you like,* the honest answer is that you'd like to be somewhere ordinary, watching someone fix a lamp, listening to a ballgame nobody's really listening to, with no problem more urgent than whether the screw you need is a number eight or a number ten.

The man would know. He'd look at it and say *ah.* And then he'd round down.
